d.title: A handler is for a failure you can see; a detector is something you can forget to write
d.caption: **A failure you can see is a different engineering problem from one you cannot.** The first needs a handler and the framework usually hands you the exception. The second needs a **detector** — code somebody decides to write, which means it can simply not exist. **So the column worth having in a failure taxonomy is the signal, not the cause**, because the cause tells you what to build and the signal tells you whether you will ever get the chance.

nodes.label: Needs a handler
nodes.sub: the framework hands it to you

d.title: The same tool and the same ToolNode, split by whose mistake it was
d.caption: The default handler is four lines and the policy is precise: **it returns the model's mistakes to the model — bad arguments, a missing field, an unknown tool name — because the model can read the error and fix the call. It propagates the tool's own exceptions, because the model cannot fix a dependency being down.** Which makes `handle_tool_errors=True` worse than it looks: **it erases the distinction, so an outage arrives as a request to “please fix your mistakes”, and the model obliges by calling again.**

d.title: Four surfaces no single call can demonstrate, all silent
d.caption: These cannot be shown by probing one call, because **in every case the run succeeds** — the supervisor treats nonsense as a result, the retriever returns its k documents, the token count looks healthy, and the request completes. **Each one needs a detector that does not exist until somebody writes it: a plausibility check, a relevance check, a fact-survival check, a cost cap.** And for cost, **the only signal is the bill.**

nodes.label: Cost: 40x what it should be
nodes.sub: 13.1 - the only signal is the bill

nodes.label: Each needs a detector you write
nodes.sub: the run succeeded in all four

d.title: Three columns, and only one of them changes what you know
d.caption: **A surface with no detection column is a surface you will find out about from a user — and five of the nine start that way.** Which also says where to spend first: **containment and recovery are satisfying to build and they only help with failures you already know about. Detection is the one that changes what you know**, and for the silent surfaces it is the only column that exists at all until you build it.

items.label: Detection: what tells you
items.sub: a schema check, 13.3's fact check, a cost cap

items.label: Containment: what stops it spreading
items.sub: a timeout, a hop budget, a breaker

d.title: Backoff alone is deterministic, so it preserves the spike
d.caption: **If 60 clients failed because a dependency was overloaded, backoff without jitter sends all 60 back at the same instant — so the dependency gets the same spike that knocked it over, 500 ms later, and again at 1 s, 2 s, 4 s.** Full jitter cuts the peak by about 85%. **Equal jitter's peak is roughly twice full jitter's: the trade is a guaranteed minimum wait for a less even spread**, worth it when each retry is expensive and you want none arriving immediately.

d.title: A deny list, so the most retryable failure is the one it declines
d.caption: **`TimeoutError` is not retried, because it subclasses `OSError`, which is on the deny list — and a timeout is the single most retryable failure there is. `AttributeError` is retried three times, because it is not on the list, so a typo in a node costs three attempts and three times the latency before failing identically.** The default's shape is defensible for a library that cannot know your dependencies, **and it is not a policy for a system that can.**

d.title: Five transitions, and the probe is singular
d.caption: **A failure in half-open re-opens immediately rather than spending the threshold again.** Without that, recovery means every waiting client hitting a dependency that has just come back up — **which knocks it over again, and now you have an outage that oscillates.** So **a breaker without half-open is not a breaker, it is a timer**: the two properties that make it work are that the probe is **singular** and that a failed probe is **immediately** disqualifying.

d.title: Safe, unsafe, and pointless are three different judgements
d.caption: **Safe** is a read, a lookup, or a model call that failed before generating. **Unsafe** is anything that already had an effect — which is 14.3, **where the measurement is that LangGraph re-runs the whole node, so a node that acts and then fails acts twice.** And **pointless** is its own category: a 400, a schema validation failure, a malformed prompt. **Retrying a deterministic failure three times costs three times as much and fails three times.**

nodes.label: Safe: a read, a lookup
nodes.sub: or a call that never generated

nodes.label: Unsafe: it already had an effect
So the predicate is a judgement per dependency

d.title: Three attempts, three emails, and the run reported success
d.caption: **LangGraph re-runs the whole node, not the part after the failure — so everything before the failing line happens again. There is no mechanism that could know which statement failed, and no way to resume a Python function in the middle.** Which makes the dangerous shape broader than it first sounds: **any node that performs an effect and then does anything that can fail — including a state write, a log, a second tool call, or a model call to summarise what it just did.**

d.title: Two attempts, one email, and the retry succeeded rather than exhausting itself
d.caption: The key did **two** things: it prevented the duplicate, **and it let the retry succeed** — attempt 2 found the key, skipped the effect and returned normally, so the node stopped at two rather than spending its budget. **The ordering is load-bearing: the key is claimed before the effect. Claiming it afterwards means a crash between the effect and the write leaves no record, so the retry sends again — the same bug with a smaller window, which is the worst kind, because it passes testing.**

d.title: A key that changes per attempt is not a key
d.caption: `uuid4()` in the node and a timestamp both fail the same way: they differ on every attempt, so nothing matches. **The subtle one is specific to agents: a deterministic key over non-deterministic arguments is not deterministic. The retry re-runs the whole node, so a model call inside it runs again — and if the model phrases the email differently or rounds the amount differently, the hash changes and the key does not match.** So the key comes from **the request**, not from anything the node generates.

nodes.label: hash(thread_id, step, action, args)
nodes.sub: or an id from the caller

nodes.label: So: from the request, not the node
nodes.sub: the node is the thing re-running

d.title: A restart is a different problem, and only two of four survive it
d.caption: A dict in memory handles the retry and loses everything on restart. **Graph state cannot even handle the retry — 9.5 means the checkpoint holds the last completed superstep, so the failed step re-runs with nothing recorded.** A store survives both. **And the external system itself is best, because it is the only guarantee that does not depend on your process** — a payment API that rejects a duplicate idempotency key needs no cooperation from your code at all.

d.title: The card is charged and nothing has shipped
d.caption: **Doing nothing leaves the customer paying for an order that does not exist — which is worse than the original failure, because the original failure was recoverable and this state is a support ticket.** That is the whole argument for compensation: not that a half-finished plan is untidy, but that the partial state is a **worse** state than either the start or the finish, and nothing in the graph will move it on its own.

d.title: Reverse order is a rule you adopt because it is cheap and always safe
d.caption: **The compensations have the steps' dependencies, inverted.** Releasing stock before refunding is harmless here — but in a system where **the refund needs the reservation record to look up the transaction**, it is not, **and reasoning about which case you are in, per plan, is more expensive than always going in reverse.** Which is usually the right trade for a recovery path: **the code least likely to be exercised and most likely to be wrong.**

nodes.label: A refund may need the reservation record
Deciding per plan costs more than the rule

d.title: A correction is a second effect, not an undo
d.caption: **An email is not compensable. Neither is a webhook delivered to a third party, a message posted to a channel, or a file written to someone else's bucket. Sending “please disregard” does not restore the previous state — the customer has now been told two things and trusts neither.** Which is why the **category** matters more than the mechanism: most of the literature is about *how* to compensate, and the part that decides whether your plan is correct is **which steps you cannot.**

nodes.label: Also: webhooks, channel posts, others' buckets
So the question is which steps you cannot undo

d.title: The handle is the part people forget, and a failed compensation is a dead letter
d.caption: 14.3's measurement applies directly — **a failed attempt's state writes are discarded, so the compensation log cannot live in graph state.** It goes to a store or a table, **written as each step completes.** And **“refund the card” is not actionable while “refund transaction `txn_8841`” is: the record has to capture whatever identifier the compensation will need, at the moment the step runs, because it may not be derivable afterwards — especially if the failure is the system that would have told you.**
